items.learnMore:
The accessibility tree

Every page has two trees built from the same markup: the DOM tree, which JS and CSS operate on, and the accessibility tree, which is what screen readers, switch devices, and voice control actually read.

Semantic elements come with a built-in role, an accessible name, and state (pressed, expanded, disabled) that populate the accessibility tree automatically. A <div> has none of that built in — its entry is just "generic," no matter how it's styled to look.
items.reflection: Think of a system you rely on that has an obvious, visible interface and a separate, less visible one serving a different kind of user (a store's shelf layout for shoppers vs. its barcode data for the warehouse system). Where else does "looks right on the surface" fail to guarantee "works right underneath"?

items.learnMore:
What styling alone doesn't fix

CSS can make a <div> look exactly like a button — same colors, same padding, same hover state. None of that touches the two things that actually make a button usable without a mouse: being reachable via Tab, and responding to Enter or Space once focused.

Reproducing both by hand means adding tabindex="0" and a keydown handler that checks for both keys — work a real <button> needs zero lines of extra code for.

items.learnMore:
The landmark set

Screen readers offer a shortcut that lets users jump directly between page regions instead of tabbing through everything linearly. That shortcut works off a specific, fixed set of landmark elements: <nav>, <main>, <header>, <footer>, and <aside>.

items.learnMore:
The decision rule, precisely

Semantic HTML isn't "use fancy tag names for style points" — it's letting the browser's built-in behavior do work that would otherwise have to be reimplemented by hand, and letting assistive technology understand structure it otherwise couldn't infer.

<div>/<span> exist for the remaining case: markup with no inherent semantic role, needed purely for styling or a JS hook. That's a real, legitimate case — just narrower than how div gets used in practice.
items.reflection: The decision rule reduces to a single testable question asked per element, rather than a blanket policy. Where else have you seen a blanket rule ('never do X', 'always do Y') turn out to be better replaced by a specific per-case question?

It meaningfully reduces the total number of CSS rules a project needs
It is a hard requirement imposed by all modern JavaScript frameworks
items.explanation: The precise argument is about leverage: native browser behavior (keyboard handling, accessibility-tree population) is free when the right tag is used, and has to be manually and imperfectly reconstructed when it isn't.

items.learnMore:
Why heading hierarchy is checkable structure, not styling

Screen readers offer a "jump by heading level" navigation mode, and some assistive tech explicitly flags skipped levels as a structural error, because sighted users get an implicit outline from font-size cues that a skipped level breaks for anyone navigating by heading semantics alone.

The check is purely structural: given a sequence of heading levels in document order, does any consecutive pair jump forward by more than one level? Going back up a level (closing a subsection) is never a skip.
items.reflection: The skip rule only cares about forward jumps, never about going back up a level — closing a subsection is always fine. Where else in a system you know (version numbers, org charts, outline numbering) does 'going back up' behave completely differently from 'jumping forward', in a way that's easy to mis-model if you don't think it through?
